title: ALMA and the centre of the Milky Way
caption: ALMA antennas and the centre of the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Ranked #50 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Several of the antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA, stand beneath the central regions of the Milky Way in this wide-field view. At the upper right glows the zodiacal light, at the lower left shines the planet Mars, and Saturn sits a little higher, towards the centre of the image.
The zodiacal light is a faint glow caused by sunlight scattering off dust in the Solar System. It shows up best from very dark places.

The antennas themselves are built to observe the sky at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, light far beyond what our eyes can detect. That makes this photograph an interesting contrast: the camera records the visible sky, while the dishes below are tuned to a completely different view of it. The picture was taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition, and it pairs two ways of seeing: a camera's view of the planets and galaxy above, and the antennas' own unseen one.

understand.summary: This is a wide-field landscape photograph at the ALMA site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and the faint zodiacal light may look brighter than they would to someone on the plateau.
